sections: Turn heavy PNGs into compact JPGs

PNG is a brilliant format for logos, screenshots and graphics, but it is the wrong choice for photographs. A photo saved as PNG can easily be 5–10 MB, while the same photo as a high-quality JPG is 500 KB–1 MB with no visible difference. That matters when an e-mail bounces, a form refuses files over 2 MB, or a web page loads slowly. {brand} converts PNG to JPG in your browser, lets you choose the quality, and fills transparent areas with any background colour you like instead of the black or jagged edges some converters produce.
Drop one PNG or hundreds. Each file is decoded and re-encoded on your own device – no upload, no waiting in a server queue, no file-size limit – and you get the JPGs individually or in one ZIP.

Progressive versus baseline JPG, and other technical details

The JPGs created here are standard baseline JPEG files with 4:2:0 chroma subsampling at normal quality settings, which is what cameras, phones and nearly every website produce. They open in every image viewer, browser, word processor, print kiosk and upload form, including very old software. Colour is stored in the sRGB colour space. PNG files with 16 bits per channel are reduced to 8 bits, which is all JPG supports and is more than enough for viewing and printing. Images with an embedded gamma or colour profile are converted to sRGB by the browser before encoding, so colours appear the same as they do when you view the PNG in your browser.
PNG vs JPG – which should you use?

table: Logos, icons, screenshots, text, line art
Slight loss each time it is re-saved

sections: A useful rule: if the image came from a camera, use JPG (or WebP). If it was drawn on a computer – a logo, a chart, a screenshot of a document – keep PNG, because JPG compression adds faint smudges around sharp edges and text. Screenshots of photos, video frames and games are in between; JPG at quality 85–90 usually works well.
Keeping file names organised

Converted files keep their original names with the extension changed to .jpg, so 'invoice-scan.png' becomes 'invoice-scan.jpg'. In a batch, the ZIP contains every converted file with its own name, ready to unzip into the same folder as the originals or a new one. If two input files have the same name, they are numbered so nothing is overwritten.
What happens to transparency?

PNG supports an alpha channel, so a logo can have a transparent background that shows whatever is behind it. JPG has no alpha channel. When converting, every partly or fully transparent pixel is blended onto the background colour you choose. Semi-transparent edges – the soft anti-aliased outline of a logo – are blended smoothly, so there is no jagged halo.

Choose the background to match where the JPG will be used: white for documents and most websites, black for dark-mode designs, or your page's exact colour for a seamless look. If you actually need transparency in a smaller file, convert to WebP instead, which supports transparency and lossy compression.
Why PNG files are so big

PNG compresses images by finding repeated patterns of pixels, which works wonderfully for flat areas of colour – a logo on white, a screenshot of a spreadsheet – but poorly for photos, where nearly every pixel is slightly different from its neighbour. A 12-megapixel photo has 36 million colour values; PNG has to store essentially all of them. JPG instead describes small blocks of the image as smooth patterns and throws away detail too fine to see, which is why it is so much smaller for photos.

Screenshots on modern high-resolution screens are also very large – a Retina MacBook or 4K monitor screenshot can be 3000–4000 pixels wide. Setting a maximum width of 1600 or 1920 while converting reduces size dramatically and still looks sharp on normal screens.
Choosing the right quality

table: Only when size matters far more than looks

sections: Quality numbers are not percentages of the original quality – they control how much detail the encoder discards. The visible difference between 90 and 100 is tiny, but the file at 100 can be twice as large.
Common reasons to convert PNG to JPG
Uploading a photo to a site that only accepts JPG or has a file-size limit.
Sending screenshots by e-mail without hitting attachment limits.
Making a website faster by replacing huge PNG photos.
Reducing the size of image-heavy documents and presentations.
Preparing images for printing services that require JPG.
Saving space on your phone or cloud storage.
Converting screenshots

Phone and desktop screenshots are saved as PNG. If the screenshot is mostly text or interface – a chat, a settings page, a spreadsheet – keep it as PNG or convert to WebP; JPG may make the text slightly fuzzy. If it is mostly a photo or video frame, JPG at quality 85 is ideal. Press Ctrl+V on this page to paste a screenshot directly from the clipboard without saving it first.
Converting PNG exports from design tools

Figma, Canva, Photoshop and PowerPoint often export PNG by default. For slides and social posts that contain photos, gradients or textures, converting the export to JPG at quality 85 typically cuts the file by 70–85% with no visible change, which makes decks and newsletters much lighter. For designs made mostly of flat colours and text – an infographic, a quote card, a chart – compare both: PNG may actually be smaller and sharper. Try one file first and check the before/after size in the download before converting a whole batch.
If the design has a transparent background and you need it on a coloured page, set the background colour to exactly the page colour (use your brand's hex code) so the JPG blends in seamlessly.
PNG to JPG for printing

Print shops and photo labs usually accept JPG and prefer it for photos because the files are manageable. Convert at quality 95 and keep the full resolution – don't set a maximum width. For artwork with large flat areas or text, ask the printer whether they accept PNG or PDF instead; some prefer lossless files for logos and line art. Check that the image has enough pixels for the print size: around 300 pixels per inch of print, so 2400×3000 pixels for an 8×10 inch print.
What about PNG files with very few colours?

Icons, pixel art and simple diagrams with only a handful of colours are often tiny as PNG – sometimes just a few kilobytes – because PNG stores repeated colours extremely efficiently. Converting these to JPG can make them larger and adds blur around edges. Keep such images as PNG, or use [Compress Image](/compress-image/), which reduces PNGs with palette compression while keeping them lossless-looking. JPG shines for photos and anything with smooth gradients and millions of colours.
Batch converting a folder

Select all files in a folder (Ctrl+A or Cmd+A in the file picker) and drop them in one go. Files are processed one after another to keep memory use low, and the ZIP keeps the original file names with a .jpg extension. On a typical laptop, a hundred 2-megapixel screenshots convert in well under a minute.
Privacy

Every step happens inside your browser tab. The image is decoded, edited and re-encoded on your own device using the browser's built-in image engine and WebAssembly, and the result is handed straight to your downloads folder. Nothing is uploaded, nothing is stored on a server and there is no queue, so private photos, ID cards, screenshots with personal data and unreleased product shots never leave your computer or phone. You can even switch off Wi‑Fi once the page has loaded and the tool keeps working.

faq.q: How do I convert PNG to JPG?
faq.a: Drop your PNG files here, keep JPG as the format and click Convert. Download the JPG or a ZIP.

faq.q: Does converting PNG to JPG reduce quality?
faq.a: Slightly, because JPG is lossy. At quality 85–90 the difference is invisible for photos. Sharp text and line art can look softer, so keep those as PNG.

faq.q: What happens to the transparent background?
faq.a: JPG cannot store transparency, so transparent areas are filled with the background colour you choose – white by default.

faq.q: How much smaller will the JPG be?
faq.a: For photos, typically 70–90% smaller. For simple graphics the saving is smaller and PNG may even be smaller.

faq.q: Can I convert many PNGs at once?
faq.a: Yes. Drop them all and download one ZIP.
No. The conversion runs in your browser and nothing is sent to a server.

faq.q: Should I use WebP instead of JPG?
faq.a: For websites, WebP is usually smaller and supports transparency. Use JPG when you need maximum compatibility.

faqKw.q: How do I convert PNG to JPG without losing quality?
